summary: Presents a problem statement for carrying mobility-related information between terminals and the network, such as signaling used to choose between heterogeneous wired and wireless access, as in IEEE 802.21. It stresses that the signaling should not depend on one link type and has transport and security needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Your phone can switch between Wi-Fi and cell service, but it needs good advice about which is best. This paper asks how to deliver that advice safely.

questions: what does the mobility service transport layer do
why does handover signaling need security
subtitle: Why handover signaling between phones and networks needs a common, secure transport layer.

tldr.problem: Devices that move between different wired and wireless networks need information, events and commands from the network to pick a good access network. Each kind of link would otherwise need its own way of carrying that signaling.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes splitting the problem in two: service-specific signaling on top, and one generic Mobility Service Transport Layer underneath that handles discovery, security, delivery and fragmentation without looking at the payload.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement only and takes no position on whether an existing protocol can be adapted or a new one is needed.

today: RFC 5164 is an Informational RFC from March 2008, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It takes no position on whether an existing protocol can be adapted or new development is required.

sections.title: The Handover Signaling Problem
sections.content:
RFC 5164 is a problem statement for exchanging information that supports handover between different kinds of links. That information can describe network characteristics, neighboring networks, indications that a handover should take place, and suggestions for target networks. The RFC says these services complement IP mobility mechanisms.

It splits the problem into two parts: the information being exchanged (information, commands, or events) and the underlying transport, which covers carrying the information, discovering peers and securing the exchange.

The first requirement comes from the Media Independent Handover (MIH) protocol being defined by IEEE 802.21. That protocol is not bound to any link layer and can work across more than one network-layer hop. The RFC wants a solution flexible enough for later MIH changes and for other mobility signaling protocols with similar patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: When your device moves, it needs to ask the network questions and get answers. This paper is about the delivery truck, not the letters inside.

sections.title: Mobility Services and Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC calls the supporting functions for MIH management Mobility Services (MoS). In IEEE 802.21 terms they are Information Services (IS), Event Services (ES) and Command Services (CS). It abbreviates a mobile node as MN, a network node as NN and a transport endpoint as EP.

Three scenarios are considered. In the first, signaling and transport both run end to end over IP between an MN and an NN. In the second, the signaling is still end to end but the MN reaches the first NN by some other transport, such as layer 2, and IP transport is used only between NNs. The RFC compares this to EAP carried over RADIUS as a backhaul. In the third, two NNs signal each other and exchange information about the status of connected terminals.

MN-to-MN signaling is not being considered. The RFC also limits itself to delivery at layer 3 or above, not link-layer-specific solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes your phone talks straight to the network, sometimes a helper passes notes along part of the way, and sometimes two network boxes just chat with each other.

sections.title: Splitting Signaling from Transport
sections.content:
The proposed model has mobility support services on top, each with its own signaling, all relayed over a generic Mobility Service Transport Layer that runs on IP. This layer is a container for the services and provides transport and security operations without regard to the meaning of the data.

The Mobility Service Transport Protocol (MSTP) message is a transport header followed by an opaque payload. MSTP does not inspect the payload. If a message is larger than the path MTU, the transport may need to fragment and reassemble it transparently. The RFC says the header definition is best handled in the IETF, while the contents of the information elements are likely the job of other standards bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a delivery company that carries sealed boxes. It never opens them, it just makes sure they arrive safely.

sections.title: Requirements on the Transport Layer
sections.content:
The RFC lists what the transport layer should handle:

  • Discovery of nodes or services, across administrative boundaries. Approaches are hard-coding, pushing information through DHCP or Router Discovery, or the MN asking dynamically.
  • Information from a trusted source, reusing existing trust such as AAA relationships or the certificates used for SEND.
  • Security association management and secure delivery with integrity and confidentiality, plus protection against replay and denial-of-service attacks.
  • Low latency: Events and Commands messages are expected at intervals of hundreds of milliseconds, while Information Service messages may come hours or days apart.
  • Reliability, either supplied by the transport or by the mobility service itself, which is hard to balance against latency.
  • Congestion control, since MIH message sizes vary from about 30 bytes to more than 64 KB.
  • Fragmentation and reassembly for long IS messages.
  • Multihoming, since a request and its response may travel over different links.
  • IPv4 and IPv6 support, including NAT traversal for IPv4 and firewall pass-through for IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The delivery service has to find the right address, prove it is trustworthy, be quick, handle big and small parcels, and work even if you move house mid-delivery.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
Information Services may not require authorization of the client, but Event and Command Services may authenticate message sources, especially mobile ones. Network-side entities will typically need to prove authority to serve visiting devices. Because bogus or modified messages could cause signaling or radio operations, delivery has to protect against tampering, spoofing and replay.

Handover messages can reveal where a user is and where they may go next, so confidentiality and integrity should be available, and identity protection should be available if possible when security associations are set up. The user should not have to reveal more identity than needed for authentication. Network nodes may also face denial-of-service attacks from MNs, so the design has to decide where to build in prevention or mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages about where you are going could let a stranger follow you, so they must be sealed and checked, and the helpers must not get overloaded by pranksters.
